extracted.intended_audience: art historians, architecture students, critics, and educated readers interested in medieval and Renaissance sculpture and iconography
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and interpreting the sculpture, iconography, workmanship, and chronological evidence of the Ducal Palace (Venetian) capitals — focusing on symbolism, expressive power, technique, and comparative evaluation with canonical exemplars (Giotto, Spenser, Renaissance copies).

rubrics_metrics.name: iconographic_attributes_and_labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures should be identified and understood by their conventional attributes and inscriptions (e.g., Humility 'with a veil... carrying a lamp' inscribed 'HUMILITAS HABITAT IN ME'; Charity with loaves and flame; Justice crowned with sword and scales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the sculptor uses the expected symbolic objects (lamp, veil, loaves, scales, compasses, mirror, anchor, etc.) and inscriptions; note misapplications (e.g., Spenser's anchor for Hope called 'as inaccurate as it is vulgar') and cases where inscriptions clarify an otherwise ambiguous figure. If inscriptions are missing or illegible, use comparative copies (Renaissance series, Giotto, Spenser) to identify figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: expressive_power_of_feature_and_gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture is judged by its 'power of expression' — the face, gesture, posture, and interaction should convey the moral/emotional state (e.g., Avarice as 'marvellous for power of expression', Envy 'pointing malignantly' with serpents and dragon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate the intensity and subtlety of expression: vivid, characteristic features (hollow eyes, strained throat, claws, serpents) denote high expressive power; caricature or coarse work denotes inferiority. Compare how gestures (pointing, tearing dress, raising hands) communicate the concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: comparative_reference_to_canonical_models
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation uses canonical exemplars (notably Giotto and Spenser) as standards of excellence and meaning (e.g., Giotto's winged Hope, Giotto's Justice weighing with a scale in each hand, Arena Chapel treatments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare composition, symbolism, and expressive qualities against Giotto and Spenser; identify where the work is 'far inferior' or where it 'gives his whole strength' to a subject. Use such comparisons to judge fidelity to medieval conceptions versus Renaissance or later vulgarizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: iconographic_fidelity_to_theological_periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish Christian versus Pagan iconographic suitability: some virtues (Hope, Charity) are 'distinctively Christian' and could not enter a Pagan scheme; Greek and medieval systems treat virtues differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the representation accords with the theological/period conventions (e.g., Hope as aspirant versus Faith as dependent; Charity depicted with flames to show love). Note when Pagan symbols are inappropriately applied to Christian virtues (or vice versa).

rubrics_metrics.name: conceptual_clarity_and_distinctiveness_of_virtue/vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Each moral concept should be distinctively and recognizably represented (e.g., Prudence's forethought, Justice's equality shown by one scale in each hand, Luxury exposing the breast with jewelled chain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for features that make the idea distinctive (forethought for Prudence, foreseeing devices like convex mirrors, Janus-headed depictions). Criticize representations that fail to emphasize the most 'truly distinctive' characters (Ruskin notes forethought is 'never enough considered or symbolized').

rubrics_metrics.name: accuracy_and_appropriateness_of_symbolic_devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols must be both technically appropriate and conceptually accurate (e.g., anchor is not an appropriate symbol for Hope; Cupid as a terror in medieval usage rather than Renaissance plaything).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag symbol misuse or vulgarization (anchors for Hope, sentimentalized Renaissance Cupid). Prefer symbols that align with original medieval meanings and avoid later popularized paraphernalia.

rubrics_metrics.name: representation_of_subtlety_and_restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should represent not only violent or overt forms of a passion but also their restrained, subtler forms (Ruskin notes absence of 'restrained Anger' as a loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the artist includes restrained or interior forms of emotions/virtues (e.g., restrained anger) as opposed to only violent caricatures; absence of restraint can be a mark against depth and truthfulness of depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_composition_to_express_narrative_and_relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement of figures, predella scenes, and companion images should form coherent narrative and relational meaning (e.g., Justice with predella of people riding securely and others dancing; Charity receiving treasure from Christ above).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sequencing and subordinate scenes for their contribution to the principal idea; judge whether subordinate elements (crowns, angels, executioner) coherently amplify the central moral meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: naturalism_and_faunal_accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals and natural details should be convincingly observed (Ruskin criticizes a 'fox, not at all like one' and admires true dead-bird renderings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score the realism and character of animals and natural motifs — accurate anatomy and life (ears, feathers, bees, etc.) indicate skill; mistaken or stylized animal forms may reduce credibility and dating reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: drapery_and_surface_treatment_as_expressive_device
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery folds and surface treatment should contribute to mood and meaning (e.g., the Moon's 'rippling' drapery to suggest moonlight on waves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how the disposition of folds and surface textures supports the intended effect (trembling moonlight, robust classical folds, or severe concealment of forms). Fine cut drapery that suggests environment or movement is praiseworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: balance_between_massiveness_and_detail_ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful capitals balance 'broad massiveness' with careful surface detail — neither overworked minutiae nor cold severity should dominate (e.g., Twentieth Capital praised for broad massiveness and minute chasing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate overall compositional weight versus intricacy: a majestic broad plan with judicious detailed chasing is preferable to mere fineness without grand form. Beware of coarseness or excessive small-scale ornament that undermines design.

rubrics_metrics.name: technical_workmanship_and_tooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of carving, undercutting, chiselling, and use of inlay indicate technical mastery (e.g., undercut fish and leaves glinting, small colored marbles inlaid with significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity of modelling, finesse of undercut, control of tools, and successful use of inlay and mixed materials. Note when defects (broken scorpion tail, broken horns) materially harm comprehension of the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_of_materials_and_color_for_effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of colored marbles, inlay, and material contrasts should be purposeful and effective (inlay in one capital expresses architect's valuation of color).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether color/inlay is legible at the intended viewing distance and whether it meaningfully enhances iconography. Small inlays may be significant historically but ineffective visually from afar.

rubrics_metrics.name: legibility_and_condition_of_inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscriptions (Latin captions, verses) are crucial for identifying figures and meanings, but erosion and rust bars often render them fragmentary ('inscriptions above... now decipherable only in fragments').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take inscriptions as primary evidence when legible; when fragmentary, present plausible readings (as Ruskin does) and cross-reference copies. Note that illegibility reduces confidence in identifications and dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: value_as_chronological_evidence_from_iconography_and_tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Depicted tools, architectural features, and costume can serve as dating evidence (e.g., depiction of 'fifth order' windows and sculptor's tools indicates early fourteenth century).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use depicted material culture (windows, hats, compasses, types of capital) as internal evidence for dating; corroborate with stylistic features. A single clearly dated artifact in a scene can be decisive for chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: preservation_and_weathering_effects_on_interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: State of preservation (defacement by wind/sea, broken figures) crucially affects interpretation and legibility of capitals ('grievously defaced' capitals; fragments remaining).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for loss and erosion when assessing iconography and workmanship; use Renaissance copies or casts where possible to restore missing content. Be cautious in firm conclusions when significant pieces are broken away.

rubrics_metrics.name: coherence_of_series_and_thematic_order
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of capitals should present a coherent thematic program (e.g., virtues and vices arranged logically; planets and Creation forming a theological/astrological statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the sequence supports a unified doctrine or narrative (judicial astrology subordinated to Christian humility, planets arranged as houses, virtues paired/opposed coherently). Discontinuities or mixing of sets should be explained (e.g., Miseria vs Misericordia reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: physiognomy_for_character_and_dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Facial types and physiognomy are used deliberately to express dignity, thoughtfulness, or vulgarity (Ruskin praises the 'thin, thoughtful, and dignified' head wearing a cap with winged lions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether facial modelling successfully conveys inner character (dignity, thoughtfulness). Skilled portraiture can elevate principal figures above surrounding work and indicate deliberate social/ethical intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: symbolic_complexity_and_layering
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective capitals combine multiple symbolic layers (planetary houses linked to Creation, moral orders interwoven with crafts and saints) to produce theological and civic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for dense but coherent symbolic programs where cosmology, virtue/vice, saints, and arts interrelate. Judge the success of synthesis: does the grouping plausibly convey intended doctrines (e.g., planets made for the service of man; subjection of fortunes to God's will)?
